turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Ellison, have a seat up on the table. I'll grab vitals before Dr. Shah comes in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I am sorry to take a slot on such a busy afternoon.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over eighty... the cuff slipped. One thirty-six over eighty-four.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Pulse is seventy-eight, respirations sixteen, oxygen ninety-seven percent. Temperature ninety-eight point six.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Those are fine for my sheet. Your aide can stay.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll stay. I'm June, I help him around the house on weekdays. The parking garage was a nightmare, I'll say that.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mr. Ellison. What brings you in?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I have an itchy rash, Doctor. It has become quite bothersome.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Where?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): The rash is on my chest and on both arms. The itching is the worst part.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, four days. Forgive me, that is not right. It has been six days.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Oh, I saw faint marks closer to two weeks ago. He didn't say a word until the itch got bad.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): You don't agree. I'll call it roughly six days to two weeks.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. It is rather hard to say.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. My breathing has been entirely normal.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Swelling of the lips or the tongue?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does the rash burn or hurt?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really. It itches, more than anything.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): New foods, new creams, new pills?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, all three, I'm afraid. I had shrimp at a dinner, I started a new cream, and I am on an antibiotic. I cannot say which of them is to blame.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Name the antibiotic.
[SEG0026] person_1 (NURSE): The bottle in his bag says amoxicillin, five hundred milligrams, twice a day.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I must correct that, if I may. The tablets are two hundred and fifty milligrams, and I take them three times a day. That is what the dentist wrote.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the dose isn't clear. I won't put a number down.
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm not even sure he takes every dose. The lunchtime one gets skipped, I think.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I believe I have taken them as directed. I would not wish to mislead you.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): How many days on it?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): For the tooth infection, five days. Well, actually, no, seven days. I started the amoxicillin a week ago today.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the cream?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Hydrocortisone, one percent, from the drugstore. I used it on a dry patch on my arm, and then this rash came along. I kept applying it, which may have been foolish.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did you open it?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I cannot give you the date. About a week, perhaps longer. I simply do not remember.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shrimp just once?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Saturday evening, at a restaurant downtown. I have eaten shrimp before without any difficulty.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Drug allergies?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None that I know of.
[SEG0041] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His sister told me he got hives from penicillin as a child. She said to treat him as allergic. It's written in a note she left with me.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not accept that. I took penicillin in college for a sore throat and I was perfectly fine. I am not allergic to penicillin.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then it stays disputed. I'm not entering a penicillin allergy.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anything else you take?
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Hydrochlorothiazide, twenty-five milligrams, every morning, for his blood pressure. I lay that one out myself.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is quite right. I take it every morning.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nausea? Diarrhea?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No, neither.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Looking now. Flat red patches on the chest and both upper arms. No blisters, no weeping. Lips are normal.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): It does look a bit angrier than it did yesterday, if I may say.
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): I can't tell if this is the antibiotic, the cream, or the shrimp. No firm label today.

[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stop the amoxicillin. The bottle dose of five hundred milligrams twice a day and the two hundred and fifty milligrams three times a day you just told me don't match, so no dose goes on the chart. Stop the hydrocortisone one percent as well, the cream you started about a week ago, maybe longer.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I will discontinue both of them today.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): For the itch, cetirizine ten milligrams... no, twenty milligrams, by mouth, once a day.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty milligrams, once daily. I shall follow that.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't settled in two weeks, we can arrange a patch test. Not ordering it now.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): That seems quite sensible.
[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks. If the rash spreads quickly or your breathing gets tight, skip the appointment and go to the emergency room.
[SEG0059] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll keep an eye on him at home.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate your directness.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): Check out with the front desk. We're done.

features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
